Snell relation & total internal reflection

Work & energy changes
Net work along a particle’s displacement equals its kinetic-energy change. In this ideal horizontal spring, only the spring does nonzero work, so Wspring=ΔK=−ΔU.

Definite integral & signed accumulation
A definite integral accumulates signed contributions. Over forward time, integrating velocity gives displacement; integrating speed gives distance. Position difference is distinct from a position coordinate.

Derivatives & instantaneous rates
A derivative is an instantaneous rate and tangent slope. For position versus time it gives signed velocity; differentiating velocity gives acceleration.

Net force & Newton’s second law
In an inertial frame with constant mass, the sum of external forces equals mass times acceleration. It determines how velocity changes, not the current velocity.

Voltage, current & power
Voltage is energy per charge; current is charge flow per time. Power is their product.

Inductor & magnetic energy
Voltage across an inductor sets the rate of current change; finite voltage cannot cause an instantaneous current jump.

Capacitor & electric energy
Current into the positive terminal changes voltage; an ideal capacitor holds its voltage at zero current.

Switches & diodes
An ideal switch opens or closes a path; a diode provides one-way conduction from anode to cathode.

Pulse-width modulation
Vary switch ON time within a fixed period. Duty is the fraction of the period spent ON.

Buck converter
CCM means inductor current never reaches zero during a cycle, not that it stays constant. With ideal components, periodic steady state and constant DC input, cycle-average output voltage ⟨Vout⟩ is D times input; instantaneous voltage can ripple.

Boost converter
Store energy in an inductor, then let source and inductor feed the output. The relation for cycle-average voltage ⟨Vout⟩ uses the ideal small-ripple periodic steady-state approximation with constant DC input, CCM (inductor current never zero) and0<D<1; instantaneous voltage can ripple.

Unit circle
A circle of radius one: a point’s horizontal and vertical coordinates define cos θ and sin θ.

Sine & cosine
Coordinates of uniform circular motion vary periodically. Amplitude, frequency and phase set the size, rate and starting point.

Complex rotation
Represent a plane point as a complex number. Multiplication by a unit-magnitude complex number rotates it; real and imaginary parts are coordinates.

Vectors & linear maps
A vector is an ordered collection of numbers. A matrix maps vectors while preserving addition and scalar multiplication.

Eigenvectors
A nonzero vector that stays on its original line under a matrix transformation, scaled by a factor λ.

Laplace transform
Analyze signals with growing or decaying complex exponentials. The region of s values where the integral converges is part of the description.

Harmonic motion
An ideal spring has a restoring force proportional and opposite to displacement. Without damping or driving, its motion is sinusoidal.

Superposition
Add signals at the same instant to form a combined signal. Applying this to a physical system requires linear behavior.

Fourier analysis
Describe a signal using sinusoidal or complex-exponential components. Periodic signals use a series; finite sampled data can use a discrete Fourier transform.

Spectrum
Describe a signal’s component amplitudes and phases by frequency. A magnitude plot alone cannot reconstruct a general signal.

Resonance
A periodically driven system may respond most strongly near a particular frequency. Damping changes the peak height and location.

Sampling & aliasing
Record a signal at fixed intervals. For an ideally band-limited signal, a sampling rate above twice its highest frequency avoids overlapping spectral copies.

LTI systems
Linearity preserves weighted combinations of inputs. Time invariance means delaying an input only delays its output.

Impulse response
The output produced by a discrete unit impulse. For an initially resting LTI system, it determines the response to any input.

Convolution
Reverse and shift one sequence, multiply it against another, then sum. Each shift produces one output value.

Frequency response
For a stable LTI system, frequency response describes steady-state sinusoidal amplitude and phase changes. Continuous time (CT) uses H(iω), with ω in rad/s; discrete time (DT) uses H(e^{iΩ}), with Ω in rad/sample.

Poles & stability
Poles describe exponential response modes. A causal continuous-time rational system is input-output stable when all transfer-function poles lie in the left half-plane.

Feedback control
Measure an output, compare it with a target, and adjust the input. Results depend on the controller, system, delay and noise.

Probability models
Use probabilities to describe possible outcomes and uncertainty. Model probabilities are distinct from observed evidence.

Bayesian updating
A prior is a probability before evidence; a posterior is its update afterward. Likelihood describes evidence under a hypothesis—in this lesson’s discrete examples it is an observation probability. Combine it with the prior and normalize; the result depends on the observation model.

Variance
The expected squared deviation from the mean, measuring spread. Its units are the square of the variable’s units.

Normal distributions & CLT
For iid samples with finite, nonzero variance, the appropriately standardized sample mean approaches a standard normal distribution as sample size grows.

Monte Carlo estimation
Estimate expectations or integrals using random-sample averages. Error depends on sampling, sample count and the variance of the quantity estimated.

Kalman filtering
Predict a state with a dynamic model, then correct it using measurements and their uncertainty. Covariance describes model uncertainty, not guaranteed real-world error.

Step 2 · h the Fingerprint

h[n]: know it, and you know the answer to every input

Now record a fingerprint. Pick a system; the first move is always the same: feed δ[n] and write the answer down as h[n]. Then feed a real signal x[n] (gray stems). By step 1, x is a sum of impulse components; if the system is linear, the answer to component k, x[k]·δ[n−k], must be x[k]·h[n−k] — that copy of h scaled by x[k]; if it is also time-invariant, every copy is shifted by k and otherwise identical. So the output is all those scaled, shifted copies of h stacked up. In the picture, each translucent mound is one copy; the orange stems are the total. Underneath is an audit: run the same input through the system’s defining equation directly, and compare the two routes point by point — the difference is reported, not asserted.

Flip, slide, multiply, add

Reduced to its bones, discrete convolution is four moves: flip the kernel, slide it into place, multiply the overlapping pairs, add them into one output number — then shift by one and repeat. Edit any number above and step through the computation one move at a time.
